common_name: Golden Boy Pear (North Florida Low-Chill Fire-Blight-Resistant Pear)
scientific_name: Pyrus communis x Pyrus pyrifolia 'Golden Boy'

planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root or container trees in late winter in deep, well-drained soil; Golden Boy needs very few chill hours and blooms early, so plant it alongside another early-blooming pear such as Pineapple, Orient, or LeConte for reliable cross-pollination.

directions: Plant in full sun in deep, well-drained soil; Golden Boy originated in Wakulla County, Florida and is believed to be an improved seedling or bud sport of LeConte, sharing that cultivar's Pyrus communis x Pyrus pyrifolia hybrid vigor. It is prized in the Deep South and Gulf Coast for a very low chill requirement and outstanding fire blight resistance, tolerating the humid, high-disease-pressure conditions of north Florida, south Georgia, and coastal Alabama and Mississippi with minimal spray intervention. Trees are precocious, often bearing within three to four years of planting. Fruit is best used for canning, preserving, and cooking rather than fresh eating, similar to LeConte and Kieffer, since the flesh can retain some grit if picked too late; harvest while still firm and green with a slight color break, then ripen indoors. Early bloom makes it vulnerable to occasional late-winter freezes in zone 7 plantings, so site it with some frost protection where possible.

common_name: Carnes Pear (North Florida Grit-Free Low-Chill Pear)

planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root or container trees in late winter in well-drained soil; Carnes blooms early (typically late March) and requires very few chill hours, so pair it with another early-blooming pear such as Pineapple or Orient for cross-pollination.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil of any texture; Carnes is a North Florida heirloom European pear selected for producing exceptionally sweet, buttery, completely grit-free flesh — a notable improvement in eating quality over grittier Deep South standbys like Kieffer and LeConte. It requires very little winter chill and shows good resistance to both fire blight and powdery mildew, making it well suited to the low-chill, high-humidity conditions of coastal zones 8 and 9 from the Florida Panhandle through the Gulf Coast. Trees bloom in late March and typically begin bearing within three years, with medium-sized yellowish-green fruit ripening by July. Fruit is excellent for fresh eating straight off the tree as well as for preserves; harvest when the fruit begins to soften at the neck and give slightly to pressure, then finish ripening at room temperature for best flavor.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Pear Varieties for Florida
